query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled post‐mechanical alloying heat treatment that drives the metastable microstructure toward an equilibrium mixture of fine intermetallic compounds will improve corrosion and high‐temperature oxidation behavior by promoting the formation of protective oxide layers.
generation.material_initial_state: A non-equilibrium, mechanically alloyed Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy with a largely metastable solid solution and minor, transient intermetallic features.
generation.intervention: Subjecting the as-mechanized alloy to a series of controlled heat treatments (varying temperature and time) to gradually induce metastable-to-equilibrium phase transitions.
generation.conditions: Alloy compositions constrained to below 6 g/cm³ density; processing performed in inert or controlled atmospheres to prevent premature oxidation; heat treatments conducted within temperature and time windows that avoid over-aging or coarsening.
generation.structural_mediator: The evolution from metastable, disordered structures to well-dispersed, equilibrium intermetallic compounds that modify the local chemical environment.
generation.mechanism: The formation of stable intermetallic phases during heat treatment is expected to alter elemental partitioning and microsegregation, thereby promoting the development of continuous, protective oxide scales (e.g., MgO/Al2O3) at high temperatures and enhancing passivation in corrosive environments.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-mechanically alloyed (baseline) state, the heat-treated alloy will exhibit lower corrosion current densities in aqueous environments and reduced mass loss in high-temperature oxidation tests due to improved oxide scale integrity.
generation.baseline: The initial as-mechanized, non-equilibrium microstructure before any heat treatment.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected only within the appropriate range of heat treatment parameters; treatments above or below these conditions may result in excessive coarsening or incomplete phase transformation, which could negate improvements in corrosion and oxidation resistance.
generation.uncertainty: Exact transformation kinetics and the resultant phase distribution may vary with specific Mg content and minor alloying elements, leading to potential variations in the protective oxide formation mechanism.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Mg-containing lightweight HEA samples using mechanical alloying. One set will remain in the as-alloyed state and the other will undergo controlled heat treatments intended to produce equilibrium intermetallic phases. Both sets will be exposed to standardized corrosion tests in NaCl solution and high-temperature oxidation tests in air.
measurements: Electrochemical corrosion tests (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization to measure corrosion current density).
High-temperature oxidation mass change measurements and oxide scale thickness evaluations (using techniques such as TGA and SEM/EDS).
Microstructural analysis before and after testing (using XRD and TEM/SEM to assess phase evolution).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in corrosion current densities and oxidation-induced mass loss (or if they display degraded rather than improved oxide scale integrity) relative to the as-mechanized baseline, then the hypothesis that controlled heat treatment-induced phase transformation improves functional properties will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Several studies have explored Mg-Zn, Mg-Ti, and Zn-Ti alloys for their potential to improve corrosion resistance and mechanical performance [,,,,]. Mg-Zn alloys have been shown to promote grain refinement and ZnO-rich surface films, with corrosion current densities (icorr) typically ranging from 10 to 100 µA/cm2 in NaCl solutions, although their poor hardness (less than ~1 GPa) limits their broader implementation []. Ti additions to Mg offer excellent corrosion resistance, often reducing icorr to the range of 1–10 µA/cm2, but are hindered by poor solubility in Mg and higher cost [,]. However, sputtered Mg-Ti films have demonstrated passivation via TiO2-rich layers and reduced current densities, although this line of study lacks bulk validation []. Binary Zn-Ti alloys have shown promising corrosion resistance (e.g., ~2 µA/cm2) and improved surface passivation due to Ti rich phases, but still face challenges in balancing degradation rate with mechanical robustness []. AbstractHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs) of the Cantor type (CoCrFeMnNi) are widely recognized as model systems for studying the relationships between composition, microstructure, and functional performance. In this study, atomized Cantor alloy powders were consolidated using spark plasma sintering (SPS) under systematically varied process parameters (temperature and dwell time). The densification behavior, microstructural evolution, and mechanical response were investigated using Archimedes’ density measurements, Vickers hardness testing, compression tests, scanning electron microscopy, and EDS mapping. The results reveal a non-linear relationship between sintering temperature and densification, with maximum relative densities obtained at 1050 °C and 1100 °C for short dwell times. Despite the ultrafast nature of SPS, grain growth was observed, particularly at elevated temperatures and extended dwell times, challenging the assumption that SPS inherently limits grain coarsening. All sintered samples retained a single-phase FCC structure with homogeneous elemental distribution, and no phase segregation or secondary precipitates were detected. reading.lever: Implement mechanical alloying with controlled heat treatments to induce and track metastable-to-equilibrium phase transitions.
reading.why: This combined processing approach, applied successfully in Mg–Ti–Zn systems, enables direct correlation of microstructural evolution with changes in corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior in lightweight HEAs.
